item.title: They Built a Shrine to Cable TV. Then Everyone Cut the Cord.
item.description:
A few miles south of downtown Denver stands a gleaming, sun-soaked building erected as a shrine to cable television.

The modern glass exterior gives little hint of the treasure trove of cultural touchstones housed inside: an MTV Moonman trophy, a “Sex and the City” telephone in the shape of a stiletto, a box of macaroni with branding from “The Sopranos.” And then there’s the giant tower right near the entrance, extending nearly three stories tall, designed to show a live feed of dozens of cable networks.

The goal was to establish a place to celebrate the popularity, power and prestige of cable TV.

“We like to say that radio and TV is the past and cable is the future,” John Malone, one of the numerous industry titans who backed the project, said shortly before construction of the building began in the late 1990s. “This will look toward the future.”

Instead, it now symbolizes the industry’s flipped fortunes.

This summer, the Cable Center sold and abandoned its 75,000-square-foot headquarters. It whittled down its giant catalog of artifacts to fit into storage and a temporary headquarters of just 8,500 square feet, an anonymous office on the fourth floor of an administrative building nearby.

The institution’s downsizing, formally because of mounting bills and lagging fund-raising, parallels the declining fortunes of cable itself. At its height, in the 2010s, more than 100 million American households had a cable subscription — more than three-quarters of the country. Even five years ago, 40 percent of all TV consumed in the United States was from a cable network, according to Nielsen.

But today, nearly half of all TV watched in the United States comes via streaming services. Just 19 percent of television viewing comes via cable.

By this summer, the remotes and splitters and stiletto telephones that once filled the center were in boxes, and the Cable Hall of Fame plaques had been removed from the walls, leaving a spare space pockmarked with nail holes.

Like the cable feeds in many houses, the video tower at their old headquarters was now dark.

The Cable Center was always supposed to be more than a repository for several thousand old remote controls and other pieces of equipment. It was educational — the center’s relationship with C-SPAN, the cable-industry-sponsored public affairs channel, gave it access to guest speakers like Hillary Clinton and John Kerry. It built an extensive oral history archive with key programmers and executives, part of a significant research library. And it was meant to be inspiring: The building, as the Cable Center’s former chief technical officer put it, was to be “state-of-the-art forever.”

The nonprofit set up its home in Denver, a hub for several cable companies as well as the industry trade news media, as the cable industry was booming in the 1990s.

It never drew the 100,000 annual attendees that its leaders had hoped for — it turns out that Denver may not have been an ideal spot for a cable museum and that cable itself “maybe was not as compelling as to draw that kind of crowd,” said Diane Christman, the president of the Syndeo Institute at the Cable Center. (The center added Syndeo, the Greek word for connection, to its name in 2023.) But the institution was on steady ground for some time.

When inquiries came in to see if the building was for sale, as one did in 2012, the Cable Center could easily turn them down.

“It’s a real, true American success story,” Ms. Christman said of the cable industry. “You have people who made fortunes, lost fortunes, made fortunes again, and who put everything into this business. There’s a lot of pride in this industry.”

Ms. Christman, who has been working at the Cable Center for 20 years and has been its leader since 2022, has been trying to secure the nonprofit’s future.

For years, the signature fund-raising event for the center was an annual banquet, the Cable Hall of Fame gala, timed each year to coincide with the so-called Cable Show, a trade conference that once anchored the industry calendar. The Cable Show brought together programmers, distributors and operators and was a key dealmaking opportunity, as well as a show of force for the sector.

The Hall of Fame dinner could draw more than 700 paying attendees; tables at the event could cost more than $20,000 each. As recently as 2015, the banquet raised $1.2 million.

But as cord-cutting and declining viewership forced many cable and media companies to consolidate, the Cable Show lost its relevance. By 2017, it was canceled outright — and the dinner dwindled to half its previous size.

Over the years, the Cable Center was forced to shrink its work force. At its high-water mark, it employed about 36 people, Ms. Christman said. Now, the employees total a third of that.

Costs were mounting, too, and the building was not living up to its technological promise. The HVAC system was frequently on the fritz, and energy bills were soaring to $22,000 a month, a daunting expense for a building with just a handful of full-time workers.

“The worst bill I recall was for $28,000, and I was having a minor heart attack,” Ms. Christman said.

Last year, when the University of Denver made an aggressive push to buy the building, Ms. Christman felt she had little choice but to take the offer. She worried about the response given that the building was such a “symbol to the industry,” she said. But she was relieved when she heard few objections to the $19.5 million sale.

“I really thought after the news broke that I was going to get a lot of phone calls and people were going to be like, ‘What did you do?’” she said. “But it didn’t happen.”

Now, she and Brian Kenny, the Cable Center’s longtime librarian, will determine exactly how to preserve cable’s history.

They know the industry — and the center — is “at a crossroads,” as Ms. Christman put it. But she isn’t giving up on the Cable Center. She is just looking for a smaller, perhaps more manageable home for it.

Cable, after all, still accounts for a fifth of all television viewing. Cable companies like Comcast, Charter and Optimum are still offering a critical service by providing broadband and internet to homes. NBCUniversal may have spun off cable networks like USA, CNBC and Syfy into a new company, but that company, Versant, remains quite profitable.

Ms. Christman insists there will be a long future for the nonprofit. The sale of the building helped secure it. “This isn’t our end,” she said. “It’s the next chapter.”

Mr. Kenny pushed off his retirement to make sure he oversaw the entire move. “You build collections to pass it forward,” he said. “That’s the whole thing.”

On one of their last visits to the old building, Ms. Christman and Mr. Kenny gestured toward a photo still hanging near the second-floor balcony. She reeled off the names of cable’s titans of yesteryear, identifying one chairman, chief executive and cable pioneer after the next in the portrait. Nearly all of them were dead.

“Brian and I can come in and can tell you the names of everybody here,” she said. “But the people who can come here and identify all these people are dwindling. That’s why the work that we do is so important.”

item.title: Taking a Chance on Self-Employment Over a Corporate 9-to-5
item.description:
When Jodi Innerfield was laid off from her marketing strategy job at Salesforce in 2024, she had already survived several stressful rounds of layoffs and been considering her longevity at big companies.

Rather than search for a role at another firm, Ms. Innerfield, 39, decided to start consulting and working with clients on her own.

It was not the career progression she had envisioned for herself. Ms. Innerfield followed what she was told was a guaranteed script for success: She went from the honor roll to the Ivy League, and then from business school to Salesforce. But the script was no longer working for her.

Many workers like Ms. Innerfield have become increasingly disenchanted working in corporate roles, as some of the country’s most profitable companies lay off workers and demand ever more of remaining employees.

Just 28 percent of workers say now is a good time to find a quality job, down from 70 percent in 2022, according to a recent Gallup poll. And they have never been more dissatisfied with their pay or their ability to get ahead, a recent survey by the New York Federal Reserve Bank found.

Discontented with large companies’ current version of work, those who choose self-employment are more likely to report having a “quality” job, according to the American Job Quality Study released by Gallup in 2025, which surveyed over 18,000 working U.S. adults.

Ms. Innerfield now works with multiple clients consulting on business to business marketing and said she was on track to surpass her Salesforce salary in her second year of self-employment. She values the autonomy and flexibility of her new lifestyle.

“Working for somebody else felt like — or was seen as — stability, because that’s what was true in my parents’ age and my grandparents’ age,” said Ms. Innerfield, who lives in Manhattan. “But that’s just not the case anymore. Nothing is stable.”

That self-employment can feel more secure than an office job tis a reflection of the current “quality jobs crisis” in the United States, said Kathryn Anne Edwards, an economist and columnist at Bloomberg.

“The dignity of workers writ large in the United States is at a low point,” she said, pointing to workplace trends like the erratic shift scheduling and frequent reorganizations that hourly and white-collar workers endure.

The reversal of work-from-home policies is also a major driver of distrust among the white-collar work force, Ms. Edwards said, and annual pay raises that aren’t keeping pace with inflation are also inspiring some workers to look outside the corporate box.

Job seekers report sending countless résumés into the digital ether or being ghosted after endless rounds of interviews. More long-term unemployed workers are giving up on looking for a new job, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“Right now, a lot of people are freelancing because of layoffs,” said Priya Rathod, workplace trends editor at Indeed. “But we’re also seeing people who still have a job, and they’re looking at everything going around them, and they’re deciding to build independence before they’re forced to.”

Self-employment has its drawbacks, of course, and success is not guaranteed. Long hours are the norm, and it may be difficult to set boundaries between work and personal time. Self-employed workers also cover their own payroll taxes and may lose access to valuable benefits including retirement contributions, paid leave, and unemployment insurance. More than half of self-employed workers say they are not contributing to a retirement account, according to the American Job Quality Study.

And then there’s health insurance. How to pay for coverage in a country with few affordable options for working age Americans is perhaps the biggest and most formidable challenge, especially as premiums keep rising. And those with medical conditions may not want to risk losing employer-sponsored health insurance.

Some workers, like Ms. Innerfield, are able to stay on their employer’s health insurance plan for up to 18 months after they leave their employer through the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985, or COBRA. In this case, the worker takes on the entire cost of the health plan premiums, which can range from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per month, depending on the plan and their family size.

Others pay for health insurance through state marketplaces, which can also cost thousands of dollars each month. Insurers are also proposing a median premium increase of 15 percent in 2027, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation. The high cost is why self-employed workers are nearly three times as likely as employees to have no health insurance, according to the Job Quality Study.

After her COBRA coverage ended, Ms. Innerfield bought marketplace coverage that has lower-cost premiums, but less comprehensive benefits. She picked a high-deductible plan that is eligible for a health savings account so that she can invest for her future medical costs.

Grace Dennison knows these challenges well. Her transition to self-employment began after her role as a merchandising director at Under Armour was eliminated last year. Post-layoff, Ms. Dennison, 42, and her husband thought long and hard about what her next move should be.

High-level merchandising jobs are few and far between in Baltimore, where they live, and Ms. Dennison did not want to uproot her family to take a job in a different city. Her husband also has worked as a public-school teacher in Baltimore for many years and qualifies for a pension, which they did not want to lose.

Ms. Dennison decided to work for herself, offering merchandising consulting services to companies and other organizations. Her freelance career is off to a slow start, she said, but she is confident that signing a couple clients will be enough for her family to reach all of their financial goals. The couple, who have one child, are lucky to be able to rely on her husband’s salary and health insurance, her severance, and savings for the time being, she said.

“I am very grateful for the financial position we are in that has allowed me time and space to pursue work outside of a traditional corporate career,” Ms. Dennison said.

For Devin Lee, working for herself was a way to make more than she ever could at an office job. After a few years working corporate jobs, she started a home organizing business from her home in Portland, Ore., in 2017. When Covid shut that business down, she started working independently as a systems strategist who helps creative agencies run more efficiently.

She has considered going back to the corporate world after feeling that she took on too much. But as she has learned more about her business’s slow and busy seasons, she has been able to make her job more sustainable.

“I say I’m allowed to have an existential crisis and quit once a year,” said Ms. Lee, 35. “I just have to hire myself back the next day.”

Ultimately, she said there was more security in running her own business than working for someone else.

“To a certain extent, I can control how much money I make,” she said. “Because if I want to make more money, I can figure out how to scale my business.

“It’s hard, but I can decide to take that path. Whereas when I’m working at a different job, it’s somebody else’s decision if I get a raise or if I get a title change.”

When it works, self-employed workers can make far more than their salaried peers, a 2025 working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research found.

Ms. Dennison prioritized retirement savings early in her career, and feels that she and her husband are in good enough shape that she can withstand a pause in retirement contributions for a short while. Ms. Innerfield established a Solo 401(k), which allows her to contribute up to $24,500 as an employee plus an additional 25 percent of compensation as an employer this year.

Another option for self-employed workers with a higher contribution limit than a traditional individual retirement account is the Simplified Employee Pension I.R.A., which has a limit of 25 percent of compensation or $72,000 in 2026, whichever is lesser.

“A $5,000 in an employer match certainly isn’t enough to get me to go back to corporate,” Ms. Innerfield joked.

item.title: Every Word My Employee Writes Reeks of A.I.
item.description:
Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. Include your name and location, or a request to remain anonymous. Letters may be edited.

Dear Work Friend,

I’m a supervisor at a small nonprofit. I regularly receive communications from a subordinate that are clearly written by artificial intelligence. Basically, anything longer than a sentence — Teams message, email — has the hallmarks of A.I. writing. This person is a capable employee and I value his work. I’m also aware that English is not his first language, though he is quite competent in English. But being sent A.I. messages, particularly about occasionally sensitive matters, leaves me feeling odd.

My question is if I should raise this with the employee and encourage him to find a different way to communicate with me — in person (which is not always possible) or by drafting his own messages.

— Anonymous

For nonnative speakers obligated by their jobs to communicate in second or third languages, A.I. has been a godsend: A program that can check, correct and polish your email prose instantaneously so that you never feel embarrassed or underprepared. But as you note, the people receiving those emails (or Slacks, or whatever) can find them unnerving. It can be hard to tell where your correspondent’s ideas end and the A.I.’s begin. And at some point, the homogenizing, inescapable voice of today’s large language models can be so slick as to feel less professional than a stilted and ungrammatical — but unquestionably human and unique — message might.

Still, I’m torn about whether or not you should raise this with your employee directly. Perhaps he’s honest and amenable to criticism. But in my experience, many people who use A.I. for functions like checking grammar or lightly polishing prose don’t see what they’re doing as “using A.I.,” and will deny that their writing is “A.I. assisted” even when it clearly is. (There’s even a vanishingly small chance that he truly isn’t using A.I., and composes emails like that only because he learned to write in English from LinkedIn posts.)

And anyway, we’re still in novel territory when it comes to A.I. in the workplace. There’s probably no official policy for your team about using A.I. to write, edit or punch up emails, so why would he know not to — and on what grounds would you be asking him to stop besides a vague sense of unease?

Or at least, there may be no policy yet. You’re a supervisor — create and enforce one. A blanket ban on using LLMs, with an emphasis on the matter of sensitive material, would communicate clearly to this employee that he needs to stop, without singling him out. (When you communicate the policy, you might include some language assuring insecure writers and nonnative speakers that they are not being judged on the quality or correctness of their prose.) It would also set a precedent for other parts of your organization that might be feeling the same pressures. As Claude might say, that wouldn’t just be good management — it’d be the load-bearing foundation of a new workplace compact.

Dear Work Friend,

I have a colleague who is not a clear or direct communicator. In person, this isn’t a huge problem because I can ask clarifying questions pretty quickly. By email, however, it creates a lot of confusion. I know he spends a lot of time crafting his messages, but the intent of them is often obscure.

Sometimes it seems that a question or request is implied but remains unstated while other times the question that is posed directly is secondary or marginal, and the real issue needs to be unearthed. This wastes a lot of time and creates a great deal of confusion.

I am a very straightforward communicator, so this situation might be particularly problematic for me, but I want to help my colleague and reduce the noise for myself and everybody else. I have asked him to be more explicit, to state his question or request as plainly as possible, many times, but it is hard for him to break his pattern. I’m not his boss, so maybe he’s uninterested in my exhortations, though he holds a relatively senior position and seems to have aspirations for higher-level work. Fixing this would clearly benefit him in the long run.

How can I make communication easier without being much more blunt? I don’t want to be rude!

— Anonymous

Well, here’s another side of the issue: A native English speaker who might benefit from running his workplace messages through A.I., which would presumably make his writing more direct.

I don’t necessarily think that’s a good idea. If you’ve already asked him to be more explicit and he hasn’t fixed the problems, there are two possibilities: Either he doesn’t really know what “being explicit” means or he doesn’t care. These seem equally likely to me. Maybe, as a lifelong indirect communicator, he’s never developed the ability to communicate clearly even when asked to do so. Or maybe he’s resentful of a peer who keeps exhorting him to abandon the communication style he prefers.

The good news is that it doesn’t really matter. The solution is the same either way: Rewrite his emails in the format you prefer. Obviously you can’t do this before he sends them, but you can do it afterward, in the form of a reply that reflects the content of his email back to him in a more direct and structured way.

For example, if he sends you three vague paragraphs with implied but never-articulated questions, send back three punchy points: “Here’s what I’m understanding you’re asking. (1) … (2) … (3) … Is that right?” If he sends you a long email with no action items attached, reply: “Do you need me to (a) approve this; (b) edit this; or (c) just read it?”

Don’t spend too much time on these replies. Their purpose is to take the work you do playing guessing games about your co-worker’s meaning and redirect it back onto him. At this point, quickly asking specific follow-ups about individual emails is likely to save you more time and energy than maintaining a broad pressure campaign to change his entire communication style.

But these emails have another purpose as well: to model for this colleague what it actually means to be direct. If the problem is that he really doesn’t understand, the experience of receiving his own words back to him in an explicit and structured format might help him grasp the practice and advantages of direct communication. And if the problem is that he feels annoyed by your urgings, he’s likely to be even more annoyed at the constant clarifying replies you send — and will change his behavior in response.

Worst-case scenario, I suppose, you could just paste his emails into A.I. yourself, and ask it what he’s trying to say.

Dear Work Friend,

I recently had surgery for cancer and am undergoing chemotherapy. Since I was diagnosed, I have learned that everyone knows someone who has or had cancer. That seems to be top of mind for them when they talk to me — they want to share these stories.

When I return to work after my leave of absence, is there a polite but firm way to let my colleagues know that I prefer not to hear stories about someone they know who has or had cancer (some of whom didn’t make it through), or their unsolicited cancer advice? I know they are well meaning, but like any other cancer patient, I have been through the wringer and just want to get on with my life with some sense of normalcy. I also will still be receiving treatment with unpleasant side effects for some time. I don’t want constant reminders of my experience through someone else’s experience. And I don’t have the patience or empathy right now to listen to a story of someone I don’t even know.

— Anonymous

If you make such a minor and understandable request, I can’t imagine anyone begrudging it — no matter the form in which it’s made. OK, to be fair, there are probably ways to phrase your preference that would rise to the level of rude, even given the circumstances. (I wouldn’t interrupt your co-workers’ stories to say something like “I don’t care about your uncle,” for example.) But your options for a firm request are pretty wide before they start to feel impolite.

The best option is to make a clear, blanket request before or upon your return to the office, so that everyone is on the same page from the beginning. The exact format will depend a bit on the culture of your workplace. In a small office where you know everyone well, an email directly from you is probably best; at other offices, it may be better to ask your supervisor or H.R. to send a short notice. The main message should be simple and straightforward: You truly appreciate the support and well wishes of your colleagues, but you’re looking forward to the normalcy of your job and would rather not talk about cancer in the office.

Making such a request pre-emptively might feel presumptuous, but you’re doing your co-workers a favor by letting them know precisely how you’d like to be treated amid a major crisis. I’m sure that people often bring up friends and relatives who’ve had cancer because they don’t really know what else to say that might rise to the occasion. If you tell them you don’t need them to say anything at all, you’re removing both a potential irritation to you and a source of anxiety for your colleagues.

And consider that in one small and useless sense, you are lucky. There are many people across the country who would like to ask their co-workers to stop talking to them about a particular topic. You now have the moral and practical standing to actually do something about it.

item.title: What to Expect at the 2026 Emmy Awards
item.description:
The Emmy Awards, being held Monday night at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles, could propel the medical drama “The Pitt” closer to the Emmy record book.

“The Pitt,” HBO Max’s hit hospital show, is the favorite to repeat in the best drama race, and if it wins, it would be the first series to win television’s most prestigious award for its first two seasons since “Mad Men” did it in 2009. The best comedy race, one of the most anticipated categories of the night, will feature a tight showdown between the freshman horror-comedy series “Widow’s Bay” and an Emmy stalwart, “Hacks.”

Prizes will be handed out in 19 categories — including dramas, comedies, reality and late-night shows — for series that aired between June 2025 and May 2026.

Here’s what to know about the ceremony:

How to watch: The broadcast begins at 8 p.m. Eastern on NBC and can be streamed live with Peacock’s “premium” plan.

Red carpet: The cable network E! will air red carpet coverage beginning at 5 p.m. Eastern. CNN and Variety will jointly host an online red carpet show for cable or CNN digital subscribers.

The host: The broadcast is being hosted by Mariska Hargitay, the longtime star of “Law & Order: SVU.” Hargitay is having a big year: she even won a pair of Emmys last weekend for “My Mom Jayne,” the documentary she made about her mother, Jayne Mansfield; she made her Broadway debut in a one-woman show, “Every Brilliant Thing”; and she was front-and-center during the Knicks’ spirited championship run. Jesse Collins, a producer of the telecast, said viewers should be prepared to see her sing and dance when she takes the Emmys stage.

The favorites: Forecasters are split over whether Emmy voters will anoint “Widow’s Bay” or give the former best comedy winner, “Hacks,” one last big victory for its swan-song season. In the limited series category, the HBO Max show “DTF St. Louis” is the slight favorite over the second season of “Beef,” the Netflix anthology series.

History on the line: If Jean Smart wins for best actress in a comedy, she will tie Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus for the most acting Emmys won by a single performer (8). Matthew Rhys is up for two acting awards: best actor in a comedy (“Widow’s Bay”) and best actor in a limited series (“The Beast in Me”). If he wins both, he will be the first actor to hit the trifecta in winning lead acting Emmys in drama, comedy and limited series. (He won the drama statuette in 2018 for “The Americans.”)

Apple goes for gold: Since 2003, only two outlets have claimed bragging rights for the most Emmys in a single year: HBO and Netflix. Apple TV currently leads HBO by three Emmys after mostly off-camera and technical awards were handed out over Labor Day weekend — Apple has 19 and HBO stands at 16 — giving the tech giant a solid lead going into Monday’s ceremony.

Shrinking slate: The TV industry remains locked in a contraction. There were 212 series considered for best drama, comedy and limited series during this Emmy cycle, a 7 percent decline compared to last year and a 39 percent drop from 2022, when the Peak TV era was thriving.
